“The issues identified through this review reinforce the case for audit firm licensing and stronger enforcement and disciplinary powers,” she said.

The KPMG scandal comes three years after it emerged that PwC shared confidential government tax policy details to win clients.

On Nov 25, Deloitte was also suspended by the state government of Western Australia from bidding for audit and information technology work for up to three months over a report the firm prepared that contained errors that appeared to be AI hallucinations.

“The WA Government remains in active discussions with Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu regarding reimbursement for the university report,” a state government spokesperson said.

Deloitte did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the suspension. REUTERS

data.title: SAP weighs cutting at least 10,000 positions in AI restructuring
data.description:
SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions to transform its software business for the artificial intelligence era, according to people familiar with the matter. 

The restructuring would affect at least 9% of the global workforce, the people said, asking not to be identified because discussions are ongoing. The total number of job cuts hasn’t been finalised and might still change after labour negotiations, they added. 

The plans come after SAP, Europe’s most valuable software company, reorganised its executive board twice in 2026 as part of a push by Chief Executive Officer Christian Klein to promote an AI-first strategy. Two of six board members will leave the Walldorf, Germany-based company in March. 

“SAP continuously reviews its organisation to ensure it remains aligned with its strategy and customer needs,” the company said in a statement, declining to comment on whether any job cuts are planned. 

As part of the changes, SAP’s leadership will continue to redesign how it develops and sells products, according to the people. Klein is seeking to embed AI tools into the company’s applications, after earlier attempts to introduce AI products faced problems.

All departments are being asked to identify areas for potential cuts, with product and engineering and sales departments in particular focus, according to the people. 

Klein took over most of the responsibilities of product lead Muhammad Alam in 2026 after he didn’t renew his contract, which ends in March. Sales chief Thomas Saueressig, who had been given an expanded role earlier in 2026, said last week he will leave the company to become CEO of Ionos Group SE. 

SAP historically has announced major restructurings in late January alongside its full-year results, most recently in 2024. Around 10,000 positions were eliminated in that effort, which cost around €3 billion (S$4.25 billion) and took over a year. It was mainly handled through voluntary departures and retraining workers, with the total number of employees remaining relatively flat as SAP hired for new positions. 

In Germany, where SAP has the largest number of employees, the labour council in 2026 negotiated an employment guarantee through 2028. SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide.

“Our headcount has increased a little bit over the course of the year,” Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam said at a Morgan Stanley conference last week, adding he “would be really surprised” if that trend didn’t reverse. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Indonesian nickel tycoon Arif Kurniawan named suspect in money laundering probe
data.description:
NEW YORK – The Indonesian attorney general’s office has named nickel trader Arif Kurniawan as a suspect in a money laundering case, after warning of irregularities in his business dealings earlier in November.

Kurniawan allegedly laundered proceeds from illegal mining and concealed the funds through intermediaries and affiliate firms between 2021 and 2026, the AGO said in a statement late on Nov 25.

The well-known trader was named in the statement only by his initials, although his identity was confirmed by authorities earlier in November.

Kurniawan denied any wrongdoing and rejected the allegations when contacted by Bloomberg News, saying all of his previous trading activities had complied with relevant laws and regulations.

Investigators have seized documents and more than US$3 million (S$3.9 million) in cash in various currencies, as well as almost 38kg of gold bars, in relation to the case, the AGO said.

A reclusive but important figure in Indonesia’s mining industry, Kurniawan has risen rapidly since leaving Glencore more than a decade ago to become the country’s top nickel ore trader.

The targeting of his sprawling mining and trading business could trigger a shake up of the wider sector, in a nation that accounts for about 60% of global supply.

Kurniawan is suspected to be outside of Indonesia, a spokesperson for the AGO said at a press conference earlier in November.

In 2024, he traded about a third of the country’s nickel ore supply, Bloomberg reported in 2025, citing a survey of industry figures. Alongside a business partner, Kurniawan also had stakes in at least 20 mining concessions spread across Indonesia. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Billions in data centre deals grind to halt after AI chip curbs
data.description:
Lenders have hit the brakes on billions of dollars in loans tied to Chinese firms ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent, as new US curbs on chip access threaten to upend Asia’s burgeoning AI debt financing market. 

While Jensen Huang’s surprise return to Nvidia buoyed AI stocks briefly earlier this week, bankers remained concerned about the legal risks of financing data centres and neoclouds potentially facing stricter US export controls.

Deals that were near the finish line are suddenly in doubt and lenders trying to sell down their exposure are struggling to find interested buyers.

Some lenders have delayed moving forward as they do more due diligence on an upsized US$6.6 billion (S$8.51 billion) loan sought by Bain Capital’s Bridge Data Centres (BDC), whose Malaysian facilities are used by clients including ByteDance, according to people involved in the discussions.

Bain referred questions to BDC, which declined to comment. ByteDance did not respond to a request for comment. 

One bank has decided to pass on a fully underwritten US$372 million loan for Partners Group-backed Digital Halo, while others are asking more questions, people familiar with those talks said.

The funds are for a data centre in Malaysia that services Alibaba and other customers, they said. Multiple banks were also reassessing a US$480 million loan for Aolani, a Singapore-based neocloud that gets business from ByteDance, separate people familiar with the matter said last week.

The companies all either did not respond to questions or declined to comment.

The Biden administration’s 2022 export restrictions on advanced US chips spawned an ecosystem of companies in South-east Asia to help Chinese technology firms access the coveted hardware remotely.

Lending to data centres in the region surged in the following years, while chip financing was just beginning to take off more recently as banks got more comfortable with the riskier deals.

That changed after the US announced last week that companies in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil will need a US government licence to purchase advanced AI chips from American manufacturers.

Globally, data centres that already lease significant compute to Chinese firms will need a separate licence to continue doing so, and have a 90-day window to obtain it.

More than a dozen bankers said their teams were waiting for answers on how the new curbs would affect borrowers and that would at the very least delay potential deals from going through.

Lenders including Citigroup and Standard Chartered, as well as Singapore’s major banks, have launched a sweeping review of data centre clients, people familiar with the matter said earlier. 

Some banks are looking to reduce certain exposure to AI and data centre debt, including through secondary loan sales and so-called significant risk transfers (SRTs).

Singapore’s United Overseas Bank is seeking an SRT deal of around US$1 billion to offload risks tied to data centre and infrastructure loans among other sectors, people familiar with the matter said. But the current news headlines are slowing progress, one of them said, adding that details are not firmed up and could change.

A representative for UOB declined to comment, citing deal confidentiality. 

Private lenders, who were the most aggressive in seeking out the higher returns associated with GPU financing, are also growing more cautious.

At least one fund has decided not to participate in a US$300 million loan to GMI Cloud, an Nvidia cloud partner, to fund chips for a Thai data centre that would be used by Tencent, according to a person familiar with the matter.

GMI Cloud and Tencent did not respond to requests for comment. 

The chill has extended beyond debt financing. DayOne Data Centers, whose biggest customer is ByteDance, has put plans for a US public listing on hold, people familiar with the matter said earlier. A consortium involving BlackRock is considering lowering its offer for a portfolio of Asia Pacific data centres, according to separate people familiar.

It is not a bad thing that the new restrictions have forced a broad re-evaluation of deals, according to Ben Kostrzewa, an international trade lawyer at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader.

Since 2023, loans to data centre companies in Asia-Pacific have soared from virtually zero to more than US$49 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

“It could be a good pause, to take stock and to review these projects, given how frothy the market has been for a while,” Kostrzewa said. “It won’t stop all these data centres being built, it won’t stop the market, but it will slow it all down.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Finding growth companies the market may have overlooked: Why culture and competitive edge matter
data.description:
The recent sell-off in US technology stocks has highlighted the risks of relying too heavily on a handful of market giants.

For investors looking beyond these familiar names, the question is where to find the next generation of growth businesses without missing out on potentially attractive returns.

Sanjay Ayer, portfolio manager of the WCM Select Global Growth Equity Fund (“WCM SGG Fund”), looks for companies with improving competitive advantages – an approach WCM SGG calls “moat trajectory” – aiming to identify them before their growth potential is widely recognised.

“It’s really the two- to five-year period, when a genuinely great business transitions from being misunderstood to widely accepted as a consensus leader,” he says.

“To identify moat trajectory, we use a forward-looking lens focused on incremental change as opposed to a backward-looking lens focused on static criteria.”

He explains that the WCM SGG Fund team uses a research exercise known as a pre-mortem to assess a company’s future prospects. Its analysts consider what could strengthen or weaken a business’s competitive position, then work backwards to identify the likely causes.

Ayer points to Amazon and Google as examples of businesses whose potential was once widely questioned.

“When I first joined the business, Google was one Yahoo innovation away from extinction. Amazon was widely perceived to be a bad business,” he recalls.

“These things seem silly now, but it goes to show that narratives and fundamentals can inflect quickly.”

Why culture matters

Beyond business fundamentals, the WCM SGG Fund team also examines something many investors may pay less attention to: corporate culture.

“We believe culture is the most understudied and underappreciated facet of investing,” says Ayer. “If you want to understand where a business is going to be in five or 10 years, you have to understand the people, the alignment, the incentives, and the adaptiveness of the culture.”

To assess these qualities, the WCM SGG Fund team employs dedicated culture research analysts who work with academics and industry practitioners. Their research combines a structured set of questions with quantitative data to evaluate whether a company’s culture could influence its long-term growth.

The importance of adaptability can be seen in Sea Limited, the group behind Shopee and Garena, which the WCM SGG Fund invests in.

After a period of aggressive expansion, Sea faced mounting pressure to improve profitability. The company responded by cutting costs, scaling back spending and sharpening its focus on its core businesses.

For the WCM SGG Fund team, Sea’s ability to change course demonstrated how an adaptable corporate culture could help a business respond to challenges and strengthen its competitive position.

As artificial intelligence reshapes industries, Ayer believes the ability to recognise and respond to change will become increasingly important.

“When you think about how companies are going to adopt AI to and strengthen their competitive advantage, we think adaptability becomes paramount,” he says.

Looking beyond the AI giants

As the WCM SGG Fund team assesses how companies adapt to AI, it also seeks out businesses that could benefit from the growing demand for the technology.

“When AI began gaining traction in early 2023, we looked closely at Nvidia, but also asked ourselves: If Nvidia succeeds, who else stands to benefit? Where are the bottlenecks in the system?” says Ayer.

This prompted the WCM SGG Fund team to look beyond chipmakers to businesses that could benefit from the growing demand for AI infrastructure, including those involved in networking, data storage, memory and power generation.

Among the companies it identified was Siemens Energy which provides equipment and services needed to support the expansion of AI-related infrastructure.

Through its research on Siemens Energy and GE Vernova, two major suppliers of gas turbines used in power generation, the WCM SGG Fund team learnt that a shortage of workers needed to build gas turbine projects was becoming a constraint.

That insight led the firm to Argan, a US company involved in constructing power generation facilities.

But the WCM SGG Fund team’s search for growth is not limited to AI. The firm is also exploring opportunities in sectors such as senior housing, aerospace and defence, and subsea infrastructure investment.

Recognising hidden portfolio risks

Looking across different industries is also part of how the WCM SGG Fund team manages investment risk.

To Ayer, risk is not simply about market volatility or the possibility of losing money. It also involves recognising blind spots that could affect a portfolio’s performance.

He identifies two common problems. The first arises when investment managers become so focused on their areas of expertise that they adopt a narrow lens and overlook important changes.

The second involves hidden correlations, where investments that appear different are exposed to the same underlying risks.

Referring to fund managers who focus on individual companies, Ayer says: “Bottom-up managers often miss that 40% or 50% of your portfolio could be tethered to interest rates. Or, speaking today, 40% to 50% of your portfolio could be tethered to a singular AI factor.”

For the WCM SGG Fund team, looking beyond the market’s biggest names and reducing reliance on US mega-cap technology stocks means asking what could make a business stronger – and what investors may have missed.

As Ayer puts it: “Will this be a better business three years from now?”

data.title: 2 Singapore tech firms previously probed over unpaid wages pay $205,000 towards CPF arrears
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Two related Singapore robotics firms that were probed after workers went for months without salary and Central Provident Fund contributions have paid $204,576 towards their CPF arrears.

One still owes contributions, while the other has interest and a composition sum to settle, the court heard on Nov 25.

Otsaw Digital paid $34,998 on Nov 25, complying with a previous court direction for it to pay $35,000. It still owes $32,719 and was given four weeks to pay the balance.

Its subsidiary, Otsaw Healthcare Robotics, paid $169,578 on Nov 24, clearing its outstanding CPF contributions. The court was told it still owed $7,977 in late payment interest and a composition sum of $1,600.

A company representative present at the Nov 25 hearing said the company’s account on the CPF portal showed late payment interest of about $3,800.

The company sought time to confirm the late payment interest and said it intended to pay the remaining sums and compound the matter. The court gave it three weeks to make the payments.

Otsaw Digital is a home-grown robotics firm. Otsaw Healthcare Robotics focuses on healthcare robotics and was referred to in earlier ST reports by its former name, Otsaw Swisslog Healthcare Robotics. The companies are based in Tampines North.

Unpaid workers

The companies reportedly first came under scrutiny in January, when the authorities said about 20 claims for unpaid wages had been lodged against them. At the same time, the companies had paid salary arrears to 13 workers, while the CPF Board had recovered part of the CPF arrears and was pursuing the rest.

Ling Ting Ming, founder and chief executive of the two firms’ parent company, Otsaw Limited, told ST then that its human resources department had been in touch with employees and was working to resolve the problem quickly.

By Feb 9, the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management had received 28 claims, and salary arrears had been paid to 16 workers. The Ministry of Manpower was investigating possible offences under the Employment Act, while CPF proceedings were before the courts.

In February, two former employees told ST they had not received all the wages owed to them and were missing out on at least six months of CPF contributions.

A former full-time staff member, who did not want to be named, told ST on Nov 25 that all CPF contributions owed to them had since been credited to their account.

Plans for US IPO fell through

Cayman Islands-registered Otsaw Limited describes itself as a developer of autonomous mobile robots and robotics solutions for areas including security, disinfection, delivery and healthcare. In July 2025, this holding company proposed a Nasdaq listing, with a plan to offer four million shares at an assumed price of US$5 each.

In a registration statement filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the group reported revenue of US$5.3 million (S$6.9 million) and a net loss of US$6.5 million. For the six months ended Oct 31, 2024, it reported revenue of US$1.8 million and a net loss of US$3.3 million.

As at Oct 31, 2024, the group had a net working capital deficit of US$12.4 million and accumulated losses of US$25.1 million.

Otsaw said there was substantial doubt about the group’s ability to continue as a going concern, citing recurring losses and limited working capital. It said the group depended on funding from operations and debt or equity sales, and that its ability to continue also depended on an undertaking by Ling to provide financial support to meet liabilities as they fell due. It later asked the SEC to withdraw its registration statement, saying it no longer planned to complete the offering and that no shares had been sold under it.

data.title: Over $9 billion of S’pore goods affected by US tariffs; trade deal will involve compromises: DPM Gan
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Singapore will continue to negotiate with the United States on lowering tariffs that threaten to hit about $9.4 billion worth of the Republic’s domestic exports, said Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, adding that any deal, however, will require some give and take.

The proposed new tariffs of up to 20% would raise the effective tariff rate on Singapore goods from 7.8% to 10.3%, said DPM Gan, who is also Minister of Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade).

Even so, Singapore will negotiate any trade pact with the country’s interests at the centre of the discussion, he told a media briefing on Nov 26.

“We also have to bear in mind that whatever agreement we arrive (at) and achieve in the US, there will be give and take. There will be compromises. There will be trade-offs that we need to be prepared to accept,” he added.

“So I think, in this process, it’s always important to remember that we will always be visible and always have Singapore’s interests at heart.”

The briefing was held a day after the US Trade Representative (USTR) proposed to impose tariffs of up to 20% on Singapore and 13 other trading partners under Section 301, accusing them of producing more goods than they would under normal, market-oriented conditions.

The duties could take effect in early 2027, though USTR Jamieson Greer offered to consider lowering the proposed rate to 10% if Singapore reaches an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with Washington.

While the new tariff will not be stacked upon the previously announced Section 301 tariffs of 12.5% related to forced labour concerns, without an ART the new tariff rate could reach up to 20%.

Gan said the Government is engaging local companies to understand and assess how to assist them.

He said he was surprised by the US trade office’s actions and report, which raised many sticking points with Singapore’s economy.

“I am very surprised that this has happened because this is not something that we expected from an important, major trading partner,” he said.

USTR targets industrial policies and CPF

Apart from the statement that announced the new tariff, the USTR also issued a 168-page investigation report listing and explaining US concerns that follow the investigation the agency started in March.

According to the USTR’s investigation report on Singapore’s industrial policies, the specific acts, policies and practices related to structural excess capacity and production include the Singapore Manufacturing 2030 plan and the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan, as well as financial support to the manufacturing sector and firms in the electronics and semiconductors, health and petrochemicals industries.

The report also cited the “encouragement of or failure to address foreign direct investments from non-market economies (NMEs), particularly China, which permits further development of structural excess capacity and production, and encouragement of or failure to address imports from NMEs, which enables Chinese firms to offload excess production”.

Singapore trade deal will involve compromises

Asked what deal can Singapore negotiate given that it already has a free trade agreement (FTA) with the US, Gan said: “It’s an open question because it’s really for us to discuss with the US to see what their concerns are.

“Whether in the process of discussion we will be able to address some of their concerns, and if we are able to do so, we hope we look forward to lower tariffs. It may not be... either 10% or 20%. It may be somewhere in between. And if we are able to arrive (at) some agreeable tariff together with the trade-offs that we have to accept, I think it’s something that will be a subject of negotiation moving forward.”

He said Singapore will be actively engaging the US administration over tariffs over the next couple of months.

Still, he said the high tariff rate and the scrutiny of Singapore’s economic policies in the USTR report were quite disappointing.

“Our bilateral relations are multi-faceted. It’s not just economics, but many other aspects as well. So I think we’ll continue to hope to be able to continue to strengthen our bilateral relationship and look forward to looking for a way to resolve differences in our tariffs and our trade relationship, and to seek better tariff for our exporters.”

The USTR report also targeted Singapore’s Central Provident Fund (CPF), a social security mechanism for retirement savings, saying the Republic uses it to promote savings and depresses consumption to boost its current account surplus.

A current account surplus occurs when a country earns more from international transactions – such as exporting goods and services, collecting investment income abroad, and receiving transfers – than it pays out to the rest of the world over a given period.

Gan said: “It will be important for us to communicate with them to explain our position to them, and we hope that they will understand what CPF is about. It’s not a scheme to suppress consumption.”

The USTR also deemed several financial support schemes for Singapore firms and the agreement with Malaysia on the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone as government interventions that promote structural excess capacity and production.

Business community weighs in

The Singapore Business Federation (SBF) is disappointed by the USTR’s determination that Singapore’s policies and practices contribute to structural excess manufacturing capacity and burden US commerce.

“We do not believe the findings accurately reflect Singapore’s market-driven economy, our role as a global trading and logistics hub, or the mutually beneficial nature of US-Singapore economic relations,” said the country’s top trade body.

SBF said the impact of the new tariff on Singapore businesses will depend on the final US action, including the products covered, tariff rates, implementation timeline, and how any new tariffs interact with existing measures.

SBF chief executive officer Kok Ping Soon said the immediate priority is to help businesses navigate these uncertainties and remain competitive.

“SBF will work closely with the business community and the Government to understand the implications and shape the necessary support,” he said.

Singapore and the US inked an FTA in 2003. In 2024, the US’ overall trade surplus with the Republic amounted to US$27 billion (S$34.8 billion). In 2025, this trade surplus with Singapore grew to US$33 billion.

However, the USTR report states: “Although Singapore has run a sizeable bilateral goods trade deficit with the United States for nearly all of the past decade, this does not outweigh the negative effects of Singapore’s outsized manufacturing sector and comparatively low consumption.”

Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at Singapore-based independent think-tank Hinrich Foundation, said if the two sides enter talks for a new deal, the US will likely demand three things: substantial new investments in the US; commitments to curb the flow of “non-market economy” (the US’ code for China) involvement in Singapore-to-US trade; and digital trade commitments that keep Singapore aligned with the US and American companies and platforms.

“Singapore will have to decide if these new commitments are worthwhile,” Elms added.

Singapore, despite its small size, is the third-largest Asian investor in the US, behind Japan and South Korea. Bilateral trade and Singapore investments in the US support some 350,000 American jobs.

About 6,600 US companies are based in Singapore, while more than 250 Singapore companies operate across 45 US states, in sectors from logistics and agribusiness to aerospace and shipbuilding.

The USTR investigation into structural excess industrial capacity that is flooding world markets with cheap exports was conducted against a total of 16 US trading partners, including Washington’s close allies Japan, the European Union (EU) and South Korea.

The USTR has not proposed tariffs on goods from Mexico and Norway at the moment.

The affected trading partners other than Singapore are China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

Some Singapore exports are also subject to US sectoral tariffs – with rates ranging from 25% to 50% – on steel, aluminium, copper and automotive parts.

SINGAPORE – It was incorporated as VFO Health and Beauty (Hong Kong) in 2018.

The company had two name changes – first to VFO Consulting (Hong Kong) in 2021, and then to VFO International Group in 2024 – and was supplying Nvidia-branded networking equipment and other computer components.

Its owner at the time was Alice Huang, former head of Megaspeed International, the Singapore-registered cloud computing firm that the US moved to blacklist on Nov 23 over possible diversion of advanced chips to China.

Trade records from risk intelligence platform Sayari identify Megaspeed’s Indonesian and Malaysian subsidiaries as VFO’s buyers.

Many shipments took place in 2024 and early 2025, when Huang was a director of VFO and remained a senior figure at Megaspeed, despite having stepped down from its board in November 2023.

The overlapping business interests raise questions about whether Huang had a role on both sides of the transactions.

Trade records

Of the 105 trade entries associated with VFO, 90 named PT Megaspeed International Indonesia as the buyer, with equipment movements recorded between May 2024 and February 2026.

Another 10 named Speedmatrix, Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary, as the buyer, with entries dating from June to August 2025.

The remaining five entries involved two other Indonesian companies.

Equipment appears to have moved in the opposite direction as well.

A separate set of trade records associated with Megaspeed shows 13 entries naming VFO as the buyer of equipment from PT Megaspeed International Indonesia.

The figures do not necessarily represent separate shipments, as a single consignment may contain multiple product entries.

Themin Suwardy, associate professor of accounting (practice) at Singapore Management University, said related-party transactions occur routinely within corporate groups, where they are treated as “left pocket, right pocket” dealings.

They are not inherently illegal, he added.

However, when an individual holds senior roles or stakes in separate entities outside the same group, it can create conflicts of interest if different shareholders are involved.

To manage this, such deals should be disclosed and priced at arm’s length, or fair market value, Suwardy said.

But as private firms such as VFO and Megaspeed rarely make such disclosures public, it is difficult to tell whether shareholders were informed or whether the transactions were priced at market rates.

Huang’s corporate trail

Huang came under media glare amid reports about her relationship with recently reinstated Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, and allegations that she was a Chinese spy.

Her business ties with Megaspeed’s former parent company 7Road Holdings date back to at least 2019, when the Hong Kong-listed Chinese gaming group entered into a one billion yuan (S$194 million) deal to acquire a gaming business from Huang and Maple Vale, a company she owned.

In March 2023, 7Road sold its Singapore subsidiary, 7Road International, with corporate records identifying Huang Le, a company incorporated in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), as its new shareholder.

Alice Huang joined its board on March 6, 2023, and the company was renamed Megaspeed International the following day.

Just eight months later, she stepped down as director, as Singaporean Tan Yong Pong and Australian Kang Kai joined the board. Megaspeed came under the ownership of Swiftdata, a Singapore company wholly owned by Tan.

Despite these changes, Huang remained the company’s CEO, chairperson and one of its key controllers, according to Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA). Megaspeed itself said Huang left the company only in August 2025.

Resigning from VFO

Huang’s formal ties to VFO also changed in 2025.

On April 10 that year, she transferred all her shares in the Hong Kong company to Linden Vale, another BVI-incorporated company, before resigning as director on June 23.

A day after her resignation, US officials conducted a post-shipment verification at Megaspeed, with Huang present. She was also interviewed by Singapore police that day, according to MHA.

VFO was renamed Pine Vale (HK) on Aug 11, 2025.

The latest Hong Kong corporate filings list Wu Qing as Pine Vale’s sole director and Linden Vale as its sole shareholder.

Corporate records also show that Linden Vale and Huang Le have listed the same address in the BVI – Craigmuir Chambers in Road Town, Tortola.

The Hong Kong filings do not disclose how much Linden Vale paid for Huang’s shares.

Whether she is the ultimate beneficial owner of Linden Vale remains unknown.

data.title: Radiant World creditor Incomlend files to withdraw lawsuit
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Singapore trade finance firm Incomlend has applied to withdraw its suit against iron ore trader Radiant World, according to a hearing schedule on the city-state’s court website.

Incomlend is among several creditors that launched legal action against Radiant World after some banks and counterparties stopped doing business with it amid allegations it falsified invoices to secure financing.

The summons for withdrawal or discontinuance is listed for hearing on Nov 30. It does not give a reason for the withdrawal, and Incomlend did not immediately respond to an e-mailed request to comment.

A Radiant World spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The trader has denied wrongdoing, and said it conducts business “to the highest commercial and legal standards”.

Incomlend provided Radiant World with over US$30 million (S$38.76 million) in credit earlier in 2026 underpinned by two invoices purportedly for sales to commodity giant Glencore, which the larger trader later told it were not genuine, according to Incomlend’s Singapore court filings.

In September, a Singapore High Court judge appointed KPMG as interim judicial managers of Radiant World’s Singapore operating entity in a case brought by creditor Mizuho Bank.

Judge Kristy Tan wrote there was enough initial evidence that Radiant World “is or is likely to become unable to pay its debts” to support the appointment.

Radiant World’s interim judicial managers did not immediately respond to an e-mailed request to comment. REUTERS

data.title: Indonesian company taking over seized forest land is Danantara unit, document shows
data.description:
JAKARTA – A new Indonesian company appointed to manage concessions seized last week from a subsidiary of a Singapore-based conglomerate is a unit of the country’s sovereign wealth fund Danantara, a document seen by Reuters showed.

The awarding of the concession is the latest sign of Danantara’s growing clout across Indonesia’s economy following its launch early in 2025, with hundreds of state firms worth more than US$1 trillion (S$1.29 trillion) now under its control.

The move comes amid President Prabowo Subianto’s drive to increase state control over the country’s vast natural resources.

The government last week revoked the forest usage permits of Riau Andalan Pulp and Paper (RAPP), a unit of Singapore-headquartered Royal Golden Eagle, which cover 338,536ha of concessions in Riau province, citing fires and other violations.

On Nov 24, it was announced the area would be managed by a previously unknown company called Garuda Adidaya Nusantara.

According to a Law Ministry document about the company reviewed by Reuters, Garuda Adidaya is 99% controlled by Danantara Asset Management and was established to engage in a wide range of forestry and plantation businesses as well as the processing of forest commodities.

It was established on Nov 19, the document shows, the same day the government issued the decree to revoke RAPP’s permits.

Neither the company’s status as a unit of Danantara nor the time when it was established has been previously reported.

Dozens of companies have been sanctioned in Indonesia in 2026 as it battled its most intense forest fire season since 2015, with an estimated 2.9 million ha of land burned across the country between January and October 2026, according to data from geomonitoring platform Nusantara Atlas.

The size of the fires that allegedly took place in RAPP’s concession remained unclear. RAPP said it had zero tolerance for burning and none of the fire incidents were caused by the company, adding that the majority of the outbreaks were suppressed within 24 hours.

Royal Golden Eagle belongs to one of Indonesia’s best-known billionaire tycoons, Sukanto Tanoto, making the RAPP seizure one of the highest-profile state takeovers.

“We respect the government’s authority and will continue to engage constructively with the relevant authorities,” a RAPP spokesperson said on Nov 25, without responding to queries about the concession being run by Garuda Adidaya.

“RAPP firmly believes that it has operated in compliance with all applicable government regulatory requirements in the management of its forestry concessions.”

A call to Garuda Adidaya’s listed phone number was unanswered. Danantara did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The local government in Riau, where the concession is located, urged Garuda Adidaya and the central government’s forestry task force to provide clarity regarding the continuation of operations on the concession and the fate of its workers.

The task force has previously pledged that no RAPP employees would be laid off. REUTERS

data.title: Bitcoin funds headed for worst month as outflows near US$5 billion
data.description:
US-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) investing in Bitcoin are heading for the worst month of outflows since their 2024 debut, as a persistent sell-off in the world’s largest cryptocurrency drives investors away.

A net US$4.71 billion (S$6 billion) has been withdrawn from the funds in November so far, according to data compiled by Bloomberg through Nov 23.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest fund holding the token, has suffered about US$4 billion of redemptions in November, also putting it on course for its worst monthly outflow.

The exodus comes as Bitcoin tumbles below US$60,000 and heads for its worst monthly performance since June 2022, when a string of corporate failures triggered a broader crypto market meltdown.

The token has dropped about 23% in November and was trading around US$59,200 as at 1pm on Nov 25 in Singapore, down about 1% in the Asia session.

The losses underscore a sharp reversal for a group of ETFs that helped propel Bitcoin higher after their US debut in January 2024.

The funds opened the cryptocurrency to a wider pool of institutional and retail investors and became an important source of demand during the bull market.

Their record redemptions are now reinforcing the current downturn as that source of buying dries up.

Bitcoin briefly recovered alongside other risk assets on Nov 23 after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, but has since surrendered all of those gains, a sign that investors are using rallies to reduce exposure.

“When a market cannot hold a rally on good news, it usually means that investors are using any strength to sell,” data analytics firm Glassnode said in a note. “Bitcoin trades round the clock and tends to be one of the first assets sold when investors want less risk.”

Bitcoin is facing numerous headwinds, from high-profile hacks that have undermined confidence in its security to the prospect of higher interest rates and greater regulatory scrutiny following the recent US midterm elections.

The absence of US demand is adding to the pressure, according to Glassnode.

“The ETFs and other institutions were an important source of demand on the way up, and there is little interest from them at these prices,” the firm said.

“A return to ETF inflows, together with net buying on Coinbase, would be the first sign that this is changing.”

Bitcoin is also facing greater competition for investor capital as money gravitates towards equities and assets offering income, according to Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer of Monarq Asset Management.

Bitcoin is “competing for the same risk capital that is going into equities right now”, Kiani told Bloomberg Television, describing the ETF exodus as “concerning”.

The cryptocurrency industry may need a fresh catalyst to revive demand after the forces that drove the previous rally have faded, she said.

“I think we do need to find a new narrative, a new catalyst, a new market, something new for the entire industry for us to become that emerging asset class again,” Kiani said.

“There are better yield-bearing assets out there at this point. So, like, why Bitcoin?” BLOOMBERG
